Here I'm using a browser.

To follow this tutorial, you need basic computer knowledge.

It's easy to follow along.

slides.title: What is a Neural Network?
slides.narration:
Have you ever wondered how computers learn?
Neural Networks help them do this.
They're inspired by our own brains.
They learn from huge amounts of data.
Then they make smart predictions.
slides.image_prompt: Stylized human brain next to a complex, interconnected digital network, representing AI learning

slides.title: The Brain Inspiration
slides.narration:
Our brains have billions of tiny cells.
We call them neurons.
These neurons connect and pass messages.
This is how we think and learn.
Neural Networks mimic this process.
slides.image_prompt: Detailed diagram of a biological neuron with dendrites, cell body, axon, and synapse clearly labeled

slides.title: Artificial Neurons (Nodes)
slides.narration:
So, an Artificial Neural Network has artificial neurons.
We call them nodes.
Each node takes in some input.
It does a simple calculation.
Then it sends out a new signal.
slides.image_prompt: Simple diagram of a single artificial neuron (node) showing multiple input lines converging, a central circle representing the node, and a single output line diverging

slides.title: Layers of a Neural Network
slides.narration:
Neural Networks are organized in layers.
First, there's an Input Layer.
It gets the raw data.
Then come one or more Hidden Layers.
These do the main processing.
Finally, there's an Output Layer.
It gives the final result.
slides.image_prompt: Simplified diagram showing three distinct vertical layers: an 'Input Layer' (left), one 'Hidden Layer' (middle), and an 'Output Layer' (right), with multiple nodes in each layer connected by lines

slides.title: Connections and Weights
slides.narration:
Nodes in different layers are connected.
Each connection has a 'weight'.
Think of weights as importance scores.
A higher weight means a stronger influence.
They help the network learn patterns.
slides.image_prompt: Diagram of two layers of nodes, with lines connecting each node from the first layer to each node in the second layer. Each connecting line has a small numerical value (e.g., 0.7, -0.2) labeled as a 'weight'

slides.title: How They Learn: Training Data
slides.narration:
How does a network learn?
We show it many examples.
This is called training data.
It makes a guess based on the data.
Then it checks if its guess is right.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of a stream of diverse training data (e.g., images of cats and dogs, text documents, numerical tables) flowing into the input layer of a neural network diagram

slides.title: Learning Process: Adjusting Weights
slides.narration:
If the guess is wrong, it calculates the 'error'.
This error helps it learn.
It adjusts the weights of its connections.
This process is called 'backpropagation'.
It's like fine-tuning its understanding.
slides.image_prompt: Diagram showing a neural network. An arrow points from the output layer back through the hidden layers towards the input, labeled 'Backpropagation'. Text highlights 'Error calculation' and 'Weights updated'

slides.title: Iterative Learning
slides.narration:
This learning cycle repeats many times.
The network sees millions of examples.
It keeps adjusting its weights.
Slowly, it gets very good at its task.
It learns to find complex patterns.
slides.image_prompt: A graph showing a descending curve titled 'Error Rate Over Epochs', illustrating that the error decreases as the network trains more. A small animation of weights on connections subtly changing over time

slides.title: Applications: Image Recognition
slides.narration:
Neural Networks are everywhere today.
They're great at image recognition.
They can identify objects in photos.
Think of facial recognition on your phone.
Or self-driving cars seeing the road.
slides.image_prompt: Image of a self-driving car on a road, with overlaid graphics showing bounding boxes identifying pedestrians, other vehicles, and traffic signs detected by its AI system

slides.title: Applications: Natural Language Processing
slides.narration:
They also understand human language.
This is Natural Language Processing.
They can translate languages instantly.
They power chatbots and virtual assistants.
It's how your phone understands you.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of a person interacting with a smartphone, showing speech bubbles with text being translated or a chatbot interface providing conversational responses

slides.title: Applications: Recommendations
slides.narration:
Ever wonder how Netflix knows what you like?
Neural Networks predict your preferences.
They recommend movies, music, or products.
This gives you a personalized experience.
It helps you discover new things.
slides.image_prompt: Screenshot of a streaming service (like Netflix) or an e-commerce website (like Amazon) displaying a highly personalized 'Recommended for You' section with various movie, show, or product suggestions

slides.title: Summary
content: Have layers of nodes and weighted connections
Learn through training and adjusting weights
slides.narration:
Let's quickly recap what we've learned.
Neural Networks mimic the human brain.
They have layers of nodes.
These nodes connect with 'weights'.
They learn by adjusting these weights.
And they're used in many AI tasks.
slides.image_prompt: Summary slide with key points listed clearly, possibly with small icons representing brain, layers, learning loop, and application examples
